title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Reproducible Ceiling/Null Result
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that compared a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator we selected K=200 tasks via a reproducible SHA‑256 sorting rule and evaluated a single shared generator output per task in both arms. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair step was never invoked (repair_applied=false for every guarded episode). All execution, scoring, and provenance artifacts are archived and hashed (notably raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4..., model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13..., task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7..., and master prompt provenance at provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...). We interpret this ceiling/null outcome as specific to the tested task/model/validator regime and provide artifact‑grounded guidance for designing failure‑rich future evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation is a promising path to reduce operator toil, but unsafe or regressive changes can immediately impact reachability and service. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architecture is widely proposed: an LLM generates candidate configuration commands, a deterministic verifier checks safety and policy constraints, and a repair module attempts to correct detected violations before apply. Prior work shows prototypes and benchmarks advocating verifier‑guided workflows (generate–validate–repair), but causal, preregistered estimates of the verifier’s marginal effect under a reproducible contract are scarce. We therefore preregistered and executed a paired experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that isolates the verifier+repair marginal effect by holding the generator output fixed across arms (shared_initial_generation). Our primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in validator pass rate per task). All run inputs, model calls, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed to permit deterministic replay (see Disclosure).
sections.related_work: Recent literature covers LLM assistance in NetOps, generate–validate–repair benchmarks, and the role of deterministic verifiers (formal/model checkers, Batfish/Veriflow variants) in operational assurance; representative citations used for positioning include Cornetto (Protogeros et al., arXiv:2604.22513) and several 2025–2026 surveys on LLMs for NetOps and agentic NetOps architectures. These works motivate verifier‑centric architectures and highlight the need for failure‑rich, workflow‑centred evaluation; our study differs by reporting a preregistered paired causal estimate grounded in a complete execution archive.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration & estimand. The experiment was preregistered before observing outcomes (preregistration id cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0bda22e...). Primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes with a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for a 95% percentile CI. Task sampling. Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and filtered to those for which the preregistered deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) declared coverage. Selection applied: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, select first K=200 unique tasks (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...). This deterministic pipeline and manifest are archived.
Design choices and their implications. To isolate verifier marginality we used a single shared initial generator call per task (shared_initial_generation); that candidate was used unchanged by both conditions. Baseline accepts candidate_c directly and scores post‑apply with the validator. Guarded runs candidate_c through the verifier first and allows up to one repair attempt if the candidate fails (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); repaired outputs would then be revalidated. The shared_initial design was preregistered and intentionally prevents generator adaptation to validator feedback—hence the experiment measures verifier+repair marginality on fixed candidates rather than interactive closed‑loop generator–verifier improvement.
Models, tooling, and provenance. Requested model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All model prompts/responses, provider call traces, scoring JSONs, normalized configurations, validator diagnostics (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshots), and asset hashes were archived; key artifact fingerprints are provided in the Disclosure and in the analysis artifacts list (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...).
Statistical considerations for degenerate outcomes. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nontrivial baseline failure rate (~0.20). When the observed baseline failure rate is zero, paired inference degenerates: no discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) produce an exact McNemar p = 1.00 and a bootstrap percentile CI that can collapse to a point mass (here [0.00,0.00]). We executed the planned bootstrap (10,000 resamples; seed=1729) and report the degenerate CI honestly rather than attempting post‑hoc reinterpretations.
sections.results:
Execution & archival summary. Planned episodes: 400 (2 arms × 200 tasks). Completed episodes: 400. Model calls used: 200 (one shared initial generator call per task; no repair calls were invoked). No failed episodes or infrastructure failures occurred. Raw results and all per‑task scoring JSONs are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4...). Representative scoring files (execution/scoring/*.json) contain validator diagnostics and are available for deterministic replay.
Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). Complete paired counts: complete_pairs = 200. Baseline validator passes = 200/200; guarded validator passes = 200/200. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 52a0858d...). Repair activity. The repair pathway was never invoked: every guarded episode records repair_applied = false in the archived scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 = 3055f874...).
Per‑task difficulty metadata & verifier coverage. The run preserved per‑task difficulty annotations and validator diagnostics in each scoring JSON under execution/scoring/*.json; these include difficulty.level (e.g., medium/hard/very_hard), parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and validator.valid flags. Representative tasks (embedded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...) show sample difficulty patterns (a small representative excerpt: medium=1, hard=2, very_hard=3 within the example set). The full per‑task metadata for all K=200 tasks is archived (execution/scoring/*.json) and can be deterministically aggregated; the archived analysis currently reports the primary paired counts and validator outcomes (n11=200 etc.). To avoid introducing unverified aggregations, we report the per‑task difficulty metadata is present and replayable rather than invent an aggregate not contained in the supplied summary artifacts. Analysts can reproduce summaries by iterating execution/scoring/*.json and counting difficulty.level values; example artifact paths and SHA‑256s are provided in the Disclosure and analysis artifacts entries.
Why the null/ceiling outcome occurred (artifact‑grounded explanation). Three artifact‑supported factors explain the observed ceiling: (1) inclusion rule bias — selection required validator coverage before sampling, biasing the task pool toward intents the validator supports (task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...); (2) the requested model (gpt-5-mini) produced candidates that respected task workflow constraints as recorded in normalized_configuration fields and validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json); (3) the shared_initial_generation design fixes generator outputs across arms and therefore prevents generator adaptation or additional repair‑triggered regeneration; because initial candidates already passed validation, the repair stage was never exercised. All supporting evidence (per‑task normalized_configuration, validator.final_state, repair_applied flags) is archived and hashed for replay.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limitations. The observed degenerate paired outcome is a valid empirical result under the preregistered contract: when baseline error rate is zero there is no room for the verifier to reduce regressions on that fixed generator output. This does not imply verifiers are useless in general; rather it identifies a ceiling regime for the tested model/task/validator combination. Key limitations (artifact‑grounded): single requested_model (gpt-5-mini; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce925...), deterministic synthetic task pool selected by validator‑coverage inclusion (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...), and the shared_initial_generation design that prevented adaptive regeneration.
Design lessons for future failure‑rich confirmatory tests (artifact‑grounded guidance). Based on the archived run we recommend:
1) Intentionally sample failure‑rich distributions (historical misconfigurations, adversarial tasks) rather than only validator‑covered intents; the task_manifest and per‑task scoring JSONs in this archive can be used to identify which intents produced validator failures in pilot runs.
2) Vary generator strength by including weaker models or perturbation of prompts so baseline error rates become nonzero and repairs are exercised; model_configuration.json is archived for exact replication of the single‑model regime.
3) Use an interactive estimand when measuring closed‑loop utility: allow generator regeneration in response to validator feedback rather than fixing a shared initial candidate. The archived shared_initial responses and provider traces illustrate how to build such an interactive protocol by enabling additional generator calls and logging them deterministically.
Statistical note on degenerate CI. When the empirical paired table contains no discordant pairs the bootstrap replicates reproduce the identical empirical counts and the percentile CI collapses to a point mass [0.00,0.00]; the exact McNemar two‑sided p equals 1.00. This is a correct and informative description of uncertainty under the exact observed data and the preregistered analysis pipeline (bootstrap parameters and seed are archived: bootstrap_resamples=10000, bootstrap_seed=1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 52a0858d...).
sections.conclusion: Under the preregistered paired contract and deterministic sampling (K=200 tasks selected by SHA‑256 intent sorting; task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...), the same shared generator outputs passed the deterministic validator in both arms: baseline = 200/200, guarded = 200/200, paired difference = 0.00, McNemar p = 1.00, bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair pathway was never invoked (repair_applied=false across execution/scoring/*.json). This ceiling/null result is reproducible from the archived artifacts (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...), but it is specific to the tested model/task/validator regime and should not be taken to imply verifiers lack utility in failure‑rich production distributions. We release the full execution and scoring artifacts and provide concrete design guidance for future evaluations to avoid ceiling regimes (sample failure‑rich tasks, vary generator strengths, consider interactive generator–verifier estimands).

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments (model fingerprint: execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce9255...).

Synthetic deterministic task pool with preregistered inclusion requiring validator coverage limits external validity to production intent distributions that include historical or adversarial misconfigurations (selection manifest SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...).

Construct validity is tied to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; if the validator omits real regression modes, the binary outcome conflates true safety with validator reach (per‑task validator traces archived under execution/scoring/*.json).

Design constraint: shared_initial_generation fixes generator outputs across arms and prevents generator adaptation; the experiment therefore measures verifier marginality on fixed candidates, not closed‑loop generator–verifier improvement.

Observed ceiling (baseline success = 100%) rendered the preregistered power calculation inapplicable; inference is descriptive and artifact‑grounded for the tested regime (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 52a0858d...).
